final_proof:
Let \(p_j=\Pr(X=j)\) and \(q_j=\Pr(Y=j)\) for every integer \(j\ge 0\). Since \(X\) and \(Y\) are nonnegative-integer-valued,
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}p_j=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q_j=1.
\]
Consequently, for every real \(s\) with \(|s|\le 1\), the series
\[
\Pi_X(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}p_js^j,
\qquad
\Pi_Y(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}q_js^j
\]
converge absolutely, because \(\sum_jp_j|s|^j\le1\) and \(\sum_jq_j|s|^j\le1\). If \(\mathbb N\) is defined to begin with \(1\), the support assumption gives \(p_0=q_0=0\), so the argument covers either convention for \(\mathbb N\).

Suppose first that the PMFs agree: \(p_j=q_j\) for every \(j\in\mathbb N\). Together with the preceding observation about \(j=0\), the two absolutely convergent defining series are termwise equal. Hence
\[
\Pi_X(s)=\Pi_Y(s)
\]
for every \(s\in[-1,1]\).

Conversely, suppose that \(\Pi_X(s)=\Pi_Y(s)\) for every \(s\in[-1,1]\). Put \(c_j=p_j-q_j\). We prove by induction on \(k\ge0\) that \(c_k=0\).

At \(s=0\), equality of the PGFs gives \(p_0=q_0\), so \(c_0=0\). Now let \(k\ge1\) and assume that \(c_j=0\) for every \(j<k\). For any \(s\) with \(0<|s|<1\), absolute convergence and the induction hypothesis give
\[
0=\Pi_X(s)-\Pi_Y(s)
 =\sum_{j=k}^{\infty}c_js^j
 =s^k\left(c_k+\sum_{j=k+1}^{\infty}c_js^{j-k}\right).
\]
Since \(s^k\ne0\), it follows that
\[
c_k=-\sum_{j=k+1}^{\infty}c_js^{j-k}.
\]
Using \(|c_j|\le p_j+q_j\) and \(|s|^{j-k}\le|s|\) for \(j>k\), we obtain
\[
|c_k|
\le \sum_{j=k+1}^{\infty}|c_j||s|^{j-k}
\le |s|\sum_{j=k+1}^{\infty}(p_j+q_j)
\le 2|s|.
\]
This inequality holds for arbitrarily small nonzero \(s\), so \(|c_k|=0\), and therefore \(p_k=q_k\). The induction proves \(p_k=q_k\) for every \(k\ge0\), in particular for every \(k\in\mathbb N\).

Thus the two PGFs agree on \([-1,1]\) if and only if the two PMFs agree.
